Class I admissions by lottery, classes II–IX through written tests
item.description:
The Ministry of Education has issued an admission guidelines for government secondary schools for the 2027 academic year.

Under the new guideline, students seeking admission to Class I will be selected through a digital lottery, while admission to Classes II to IX will be based on written tests.

The ministry issued the guidelines on Tuesday. Applicants seeking admission to Class I may list up to five preferred schools. However, if an applicant selects both shifts at a school operating in two shifts, the two shifts will count as two separate choices.

The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) will centrally manage the digital lottery process for Class I admissions.

For Classes II to IX, students will be selected for vacant seats through written examinations, with admission determined by merit ranking. The admission test will carry 50 marks for Classes II to V and 100 marks for Classes VI to IX.

At a press conference in March, Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon announced that examinations would replace the lottery system for school admissions. Since then, educationists and other stakeholders have warned that introducing admission tests, particularly at the primary level, could put unnecessary pressure on children. They have also cautioned that it could increase dependence on coaching centres and private tuition, further widening inequalities in the education system. Allegations have already emerged that coaching activities have begun in different parts of Dhaka in preparation for the admission tests.

A subsequent decision was made to retain the lottery system for Class I admissions while introducing examinations for higher classes. Later, discussions were held on whether schools under the Ministry of Education could continue using the lottery system for Classes I to V, as before. However, that proposal was not adopted.

In the past, children had to face intense competition at a very young age in the name of school admission tests. Coaching centres and private tuition were common, and many families turned to coaching centres to secure places for their children in reputed schools. There were also allegations of irregularities, corruption and nepotism in the admission process. As a result, admission to good schools was difficult for many students from ordinary and low-income families. The issue had been widely debated in the media for years.

Against this backdrop, the lottery system was initially introduced only for Class I. From the 2011 academic year, government secondary schools offering Class I were required to admit students through a lottery instead of an admission test. The same system was introduced in private schools the following year. However, admissions to Classes II to IX continued to be conducted through examinations.

Later, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the lottery system was introduced for all classes for the 2021 academic year. The practice continued thereafter. The latest guidelines now marks a change to that arrangement.

item.title: NYT, The Economist and AFP join AI copyright coalition
item.description:
Forty major media groups including The New York Times, The Economist and Agence France-Presse (AFP) have joined a global coalition of publishers that is seeking to prevent AI companies from using their journalism without permission, the group announced on Tuesday.

The coalition, known as SPUR (Standards for Publisher Usage Rights), was launched in February and already included media groups such as the BBC, The Financial Times and the Associated Press news agency as members.

The latest expansion doubles the number of publishers taking part, with the coalition aiming to help media companies track their content, highlight illegal copyright theft, and negotiate commercial deals with the AI groups behind services such as ChatGPT or Claude.

"There is rapidly growing momentum behind our effort to build a fairer, more sustainable information economy," David Buttle, co-founder and spokesperson for the SPUR Coalition, said in a statement.

"We know that high-quality journalism forms the foundations of AI models yet, as it stands, publishers have no mechanism to ensure they are fairly compensated for their work."

Fabrice Fries, the chairman and chief executive officer of Agence France-Presse (AFP), stressed that "each day, millions of people rely on AI assistants for information gathered and verified by news agency journalists."

"That original journalistic value must be recognised, credited and fairly compensated. Content traceability is not only a matter of intellectual property; it is also essential to maintaining public trust," he added in a statement.

Buttle called AFP''s decision to join the coalition "an important step in our growth".

"AFP is one of the world''s leading news agencies, and its journalism is of tremendous value to those developing AI systems. Too often, that value is captured without permission or compensation," he added.

Other news organisations which joined on Tuesday include US-based The Atlantic and Britain''s The Observer newspaper, Radio France, as well as publishers'' associations from Brazil, Japan, Argentina and Colombia.

Obtaining remuneration for their content is a vital issue for publishers whose traditional advertising-based business model has been undercut by social networks.

AI sites have also reduced the number of users going to internet news sites.

The New York Times sued OpenAI -- the maker of ChatGPT -- three years ago in a New York federal court for alleged theft of its copyrighted material used to train the company''s text-generating AI models.

The newspaper has accused OpenAI of committing "an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions" by using millions of news articles.

OpenAI has since signed content licensing deals with some news publishers around the world including The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, Le Monde in France and The Telegraph in Britain.

item.title: Ex-advisers condemn harassment of Prof Yunus at New York airport
item.description:
Former advisers to the interim government, led by Prof Muhammad Yunus, have strongly condemned “persistent harassment, online smear campaigns and targeted attacks” against the former chief adviser, including alleged harassment at New York airport.
“We express our unreserved outrage and strongest possible condemnation regarding the persistent harassment, online smear campaigns, and targeted attacks directed at former Chief Adviser, Nobel Laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus,” reads a joint statement issued by them on Tuesday.
The former advisers said the interim government did its best in addressing the Herculean task of rebuilding a nation at a time when Bangladesh stood on the precipice of total collapse following years of “unrestrained economic plunder, collapse of democratic institutions and corruption, systemic tyranny and gross violation of human rights”.
They claimed that the interim government put an end to heinous practices like enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings that were regularly committed under the fascist regime.
In February 2026, the interim government handed over power to a government elected through a free and fair general election, with the hope that the process of rebuilding the democratic institutions, ensuring justice for the victims of the fascist regime and defending human rights will continue in a sustained manner, the signatories said.
“​It is with deep regret that we notice that some political miscreants and a vested quarter are relentlessly spreading malicious misinformation and physically threatening Prof Yunus. We strongly condemn such cowardly tactics designed to create instability and undermine the credibility and wide acceptance of the interim government,” the statement reads.
The former advisers stated unequivocally that no amount of intimidation, falsehoods, online harassment, or personal threats will ever break their resolve for the changes July promised.
​The historic mandate of reform and dignity achieved by the people of Bangladesh and through enormous sacrifice of the youth cannot and will not be erased by malicious propaganda and attempts of an ousted fascist regime and its supporters, they said.
The signatories are former advisers Dr Salehuddin Ahmed, Dr M Fouzul Kabir Khan, CR Abrar, Dr Asif Nazrul, Adilur Rahman Khan, Lt Gen (retd) Jahangir Alam Choudhury, Brig Gen (retd) Dr Sakhawat Hussain, Faruk E Azam, Farida Akhter, Sharmeen Murshid, Mostofa Sarwar Farooki and Syeda Rizwana Hasan.
An attempt was made to harass Prof Yunus at the John F Kennedy Airport in New York, the United States, on Monday.

item.title: DC, SP rescue CUET VC after 30-hour confinement
item.description:
Vice-Chancellor of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam was rescued by the Chittagong deputy commissioner and police superintendent on Tuesday evening after remaining confined to an administrative building for nearly 30 hours amid a student protest.
He was taken to Chittagong city for medical treatment.
Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Zahidul Islam Mia and Superintendent of Police Mohammad Masud Alam rescued the vice-chancellor from Administrative Building-2 at around 6:00pm.
Earlier, at around 5:20pm, the two officials and other administration representatives arrived on the campus and held talks with the protesting students. They entered the building at around 5:50pm.
The deputy commissioner said they had come to ensure proper medical treatment for the vice-chancellor, who had fallen ill after being deprived of water and electricity for an extended period. He also assured the students that their demands would be conveyed to the government.
“He felt unwell after being without water and electricity for a prolonged period. Doctors have also advised him to receive advanced medical treatment. He contacted us by phone and through a live broadcast, seeking our assistance. We have come to take him for better treatment,” Zahidul Islam Mia said.
He added that the government was aware of the crisis on campus and expressed hope that it would be resolved soon.
The vice-chancellor and 11 others had remained confined to the building for nearly 30 hours without water, electricity or food supplies.
On September 21, Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam of Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) was appointed CUET vice-chancellor, replacing Professor Abu Sadat Mohammad Sayem.
Since September 22, students have been enforcing a “complete shutdown” programme demanding Sayem’s reinstatement. Teachers, officers and employees have also been observing work abstentions in support of the demand, bringing classes and examinations to a halt.
The new vice-chancellor had been unable to enter the campus following his appointment because of the protests. On Monday, however, he entered his office in the vice-chancellor’s building after breaking a lock placed by students, accompanied by leaders of the CUET unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal.
After learning of his arrival, students began gathering outside his office at around 9:30am and gave him a deadline to leave. When the deadline expired, they locked the building’s gate again at around noon and disconnected its water and electricity supplies.
The protesting students said they would remove the lock only if the vice-chancellor resigned, allowing him to leave the campus with dignity.

item.title: Prof Yunus’ harassment in US: New York Mission asked to take due legal action
item.description:
Strongly condemning the harassment of former interim government Chief Adviser Professor Dr Muhammad Yunus at John F Kennedy Airport in New York, US, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has asked its Mission in New York to take up the matter with local law enforcing agencies.
The MoFA, in a statement, also said it asked the Bangladesh Mission in New York to identify the perpetrators and take due legal action against those who have tarnished the image of Bangladesh and all its citizens before the world.
“The government of Bangladesh strongly condemns the harassment of former interim government chief adviser Professor Dr Muhammad Yunus at John F Kennedy Airport in New York, US,” said the ministry.
It appears that a group of perpetrators suspected to be linked with the Bangladesh Awami League, were behind this harassment committed against Nobel Peace Prize laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus on foreign soil, the government said, noting that Prof Yunus is highly respected by the international community.
Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said the government will take necessary measures over the harassment of Prof Yunus.
Any attempt by Awami League leaders or activists living abroad to engage in such acts would not go unchallenged, he said at a press briefing on the progress of various government activities at Secretariat.
Dr Yunus is currently in the US, where an attempt was made to harass him at an airport, he said, adding that the incident is believed to be linked to Dr Yunus taking responsibility for running the state after Sheikh Hasina fled the country.

item.description:

item.title: Milon: SSC re-exams planned within 15 days for students failing in up to two subjects
item.description:
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon on Tuesday said the government plans to arrange re-examinations within 15 days of the publication of SSC results for students who fail in up to two subjects.
“The government also plans to help students struggling in general education transition to technical and vocational education, rather than allowing them to continue facing academic setbacks,” he said while speaking to journalists at the auditorium of the Rural Development Academy (RDA) in Bogra.
The minister said the government wants to expand skills-based education opportunities for students who fall behind in the general education system. Cultural activities, sports, and recreation would receive greater emphasis alongside academic studies from Class IV, aiming to ensure children develop both physically and mentally, he added.
Earlier at noon, Milon attended an orientation training course for 612 officers who joined the 49th Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) general education cadre as the chief guest.
Addressing the newly appointed officers, he stressed the need to address teacher shortages and gain professional experience in rural areas. He also urged teachers to encourage students to ask questions and place greater emphasis on research-based teaching.
Describing government colleges as institutions that provide higher education opportunities to the general public, the minister said the country's future would depend largely on teachers' sense of responsibility.
He also reaffirmed the government's commitment to prioritizing education and called for preventing the waste of public funds allocated to the sector.
The program was chaired by Dr Sardar Md Keramat Ali, secretary (routine duties) of the Secondary and Higher Education Division.
Bogra-6 (Sadar) MP Rezaul Karim Badsha, Prof Dr Wasim Md Mezbahul Haque, director general of the National Academy for Educational Management (NAEM), Prof Dr Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel, director general of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, and Dr Md Abdul Majid Pramanik, acting director general of RDA, Bogra, also addressed the event.

item.title: Dr Zahid: State responsible for supporting all regardless of ethnicity, religion
item.description:
Women and Children Affairs and Social Welfare Minister Prof Dr AZM Zahid Hossain on Tuesday said the state has a responsibility to stand beside all people, irrespective of their ethnicity, religion or colour.
He said the government is working in a coordinated manner to ensure the welfare and rights of all people in society, including children with disabilities.
The minister made the remarks while addressing a program marking World Cerebral Palsy Day 2026 and distributing special grant cheques, organized by the Neuro-Developmental Disability Protection Trust at the Bangladesh Social Welfare Council in Eskaton in the capital.
Highlighting the importance of ensuring the mental and physical well-being of parents and caregivers of children with special needs, Zahid said family members, particularly mothers, often have to work tirelessly day and night to provide round-the-clock care for their children.
Supporting the large number of parents and caregivers is also a key priority of the state, he said, adding that the government is working to make education, skills development and rehabilitation programs for children with disabilities more effective and sustainable.
Emphasizing the need to protect the rights of people with special needs through urban planning and infrastructure development, the minister said ramps should be installed in large buildings and shopping malls to ensure accessibility.
He also stressed the need to make public transport accessible to people with special needs.
Calling for greater sensitivity towards them, Dr Zahid urged public transport drivers and assistants to behave respectfully and sensitively towards people with disability. He also called on the general public to demonstrate empathy and understanding.
Stressing the role of the media in raising awareness, the minister said people often hesitate to speak openly about various social problems and realities.
Mainstream media and social media users should play a responsible role in raising public awareness by presenting these issues from a positive perspective, he added.
At the program, the minister distributed special grant cheques among 50 children with disabilities affected by cerebral palsy.
The event concluded with a cultural performance by children with disabilities.
Social Welfare Secretary Dr Mohammad Abu Yusuf presided over the program, while Executive Secretary of the Social Welfare Council Md Kamruzzaman Dulal attended as a special guest.
Managing Director of the trust Shamima Ferdous delivered the welcome address.
Professor Dr Md Mizanur Rahman, former chairman of the Department of Paediatric Neurology at Bangladesh Medical University and Dr Shaoli Sarkar, a paediatric neurologist at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital, presented the keynote paper on neuro-developmental disability (NDD) protection and prevention in observance of World Cerebral Palsy Day.
Children with disabilities, their parents, senior officials of the relevant ministry and representatives of social welfare organizations were also present.

item.title: Admission tests return to govt schools, class I gets lottery
item.description:
The government has decided to introduce written admission tests for Classes II–IX at government secondary schools for the 2027 academic year, while students seeking admission to Class I will be selected through a digital lottery. Under the new admission policy, applicants for Class I can list up to five schools in order of preference. The admission test will carry 50 marks for Classes II–V and 100 marks for Classes VI–IX.
The Secondary and Higher Education Division of the Ministry of Education issued the Government Secondary School Student Admission Policy-2027 on Tuesday.
According to the policy, applications, fee collection, result processing and publication will be conducted online for government secondary schools across the country.
The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) will conduct a centralised digital lottery to select students for Class I. For Classes II–IX, students will be admitted to vacant seats based on merit through written examinations.
The policy states that, in line with the National Education Policy 2010, students should generally be at least six years old to enter Class I. However, applicants must be between five and seven years old as of January 1, 2027.
Students with special needs may receive an additional age relaxation of up to five years.
The academic year will run from January 1 to December 31, with a maximum of 55 students in each class section. Admissions will be offered to the entry-level class of each government secondary school and up to Class IX, subject to seat availability.
The admission test for Classes II–V will carry 50 marks, comprising 15 marks for Bangla, 15 for English and 20 for mathematics. The examination will last one hour.
For Classes VI–IX, the test will carry 100 marks, with 30 marks each for Bangla and English and 40 for mathematics. The examination will last two hours.
Questions must be based on National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) textbooks for the respective classes. The policy also directs authorities to maintain the highest levels of confidentiality and security during question-paper preparation and moderation. Authorities must prepare waiting lists alongside the lists of students selected through the written examinations. Each waiting list must contain as many candidates as there are vacant seats.
If a selected student fails to complete admission within the stipulated deadline, candidates will be admitted sequentially from the waiting list.
The government has set the online application fee at a maximum of Tk 110 for Class I and Tk 250 for Classes II–IX under the new admission policy.
Admission fees, including session charges, must be determined in line with the Ministry of Education’s directives.
Before the Class I lottery, the software must be tested by another government-approved technical institution to verify its accuracy. The relevant certification must be preserved.
The list of lottery-selected students must be published on the respective school’s website and displayed on its notice board. No student outside the published list may be admitted.
Government secondary schools in Dhaka city will reserve 40% of their seats for students from designated catchment areas, while the remaining 60% will remain open to all applicants.
The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) will determine the catchment areas for the schools and notify the relevant authorities.
The policy also reserves 10% of Class VI seats for students who have passed Class V at independent government primary schools.
Other reserved quotas include 5% for children of freedom fighters and martyred freedom fighters, 2% for students with special needs, 1% for children of officials and employees of the Ministry of Education, and another 1% for children of officials and employees of departments and agencies under the ministry.
In addition, 3% of seats will be reserved for siblings and 2% for twins.
If no eligible applicants are available under any reserved category, the vacant seats must be filled by general applicants in accordance with the policy. No seat can be left vacant.
The government has introduced a provision to reserve an additional 5% of seats in each class section for the children of government officials and employees transferred to new workplaces.
Applicants must submit an application, along with the necessary supporting documents, to the admission committee chair within 12 months of the transfer order.
In Dhaka city, city corporation areas and divisional cities, admission to a government or private secondary school near the new workplace will be allowed if the transfer places the employee more than 10 kilometres from their previous workplace. In districts, upazilas and thanas, admission will be allowed to a school near the new workplace.
Additional seats will also be reserved at government secondary schools for the eligible children of their own teachers and employees. If the school does not offer the appropriate class, arrangements must be made to reserve a seat at a nearby suitable school.

item.title: Saudi coalition tells Sanaa residents to flee site before operation
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition signaled an imminent attack on an oil facility in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital on Tuesday, warning civilians in the surrounding area to get out.
After a series of attacks on the kingdom’s airports and oil facilities, it was the first time the coalition battling the Houthis has issued an evacuation order for Yemen’s Sanaa since their war flared up again in July.
The coalition demanded “that civilians evacuate the site of the Yemen Petroleum Company, the al-Sabaha Central Station in Sanaa... for their own safety,” said spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X, referring to a site on the western outskirts of the capital.
The Houthis issued a swift warning that a strike would be met with a “tough and painful response”, telling employees to evacuate Saudi oil giant Aramco facilities and threatening to hit Riyadh’s international airport, which they struck several times in the past week.
An attack there on Saturday left 13 people dead, rocking the world’s top crude oil exporter and deepening the war in Yemen, where it backs the internationally recognized government.
The kingdom was still weathering fresh attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of Riyadh.
Many countries have since issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday.
The Saudi coalition has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, in a long-running civil war against the Houthis that has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists in the capital.
Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Its GDP is expected to shrink by 3.3%, it said in its latest World Economic Outlook report, compiled before the attack on Riyadh’s international airport.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran’s chokehold on Hormuz, a vital shipping route for oil and gas, since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the restart in July of Yemen’s frozen civil war, pitting a Saudi-led coalition backing the government against the rival Houthis, has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea -- Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route.
Blasts resounded over the Saudi capital again late on Monday, with the Saudi coalition saying it had intercepted a Houthi missile and the group announcing it had once again targeted the airport, whose operations remain suspended.
In the evening, mobile phones received a government alert warning of a “hostile aerial threat,” before the announcement of the interception.
On Monday evening, as text messages warning of an attack were sent across the Saudi capital, Human Resources Minister Ahmad bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi remained defiant at an economic forum.
“We’re not going out,” he told the crowd at the Riyadh Economic Forum after looking at his phone. “We are safe. With God’s will. May God turn their plots back against them.”
The Riyadh airport attack prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, after having reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom.
The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position.”
Since the Middle East war began, Tehran has sought to impose its control over the Strait of Hormuz, repeatedly attacking ships that transit without its authorization.
The US has imposed its own counter-blockade on Iranian ports, and has escorted friendly ships through the waterway in increasing numbers.
Saudi Arabia has used its East-West oil pipeline to bypass the Hormuz strait and send crude to its Red Sea coast.
However, the pipeline was temporarily shut in September after it was hit by strikes blamed on Iran-backed groups in Iraq.

item.title: Ivy gets bail in murder case in Narayanganj
item.description:
A court in Narayanganj on Tuesday granted bail to former Narayanganj City Corporation Mayor and Awami League leader Selina Hayat Ivy in a murder case filed over the killing of a rickshaw puller during the July 2024 uprising.
Narayanganj District and Sessions Judge Abu Shamim Azad passed the order when Ivy appeared before the court with a bail prayer.
Ivy earlier secured bail from the High Court in the case.
The case was filed over the killing of rickshaw puller Tuhin, who was shot dead in front of Dutch-Bangla Bank in the Shimrail area of Siddhirganj on the Dhaka-Chittagong highway on July 20, 2024.
Tuhin’s wife Aleya Akter Mim filed the case with Siddhirganj Police Station on September 13, 2024.
A total of 99 people, including former MPs AKM Shamim Osman and Golam Dastagir Gazi, Shamim Osman's son Ayon Osman and nephew Azmeri Osman, were named accused in the case. Ivy was listed as the 11th accused.
Ivy was surrounded by party activists as she headed towards her vehicle from the court after getting bail.
She raised the slogan, "Joy Bangla cannot be suppressed, Joy Bangla," before getting into her car, with the activists joining her in chanting the slogan.

item.title: Car driven by DU teacher’s son hits 7 students on campus
item.description:
Seven Dhaka University (DU) students were injured after a private car hit them on campus on Tuesday morning.
Six of the injured are from the Department of Marketing and one from the Department of Linguistics. They were taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), where one student was reported to be in critical condition.
The accident occurred around 11am when Sadman Sakib, a student of the university’s Institute of Information Technology for the 2023-24 academic year, was driving the car. He is the son of Dr Md Shahidul Islam, a teacher at the Department of Mathematics.
According to witnesses, Sadman lost control of the car while learning to drive and hit the students. Some were riding in rickshaws, while others were standing near a gate adjacent to the Faculty of Business Studies (FBS) and Mall Chattar.
Following the accident, students detained Sadman and took him to the university proctor’s office.
Sadman said he had taken the car out despite having little driving experience. A driver was accompanying him.
“I drove around the Arts Building once and was approaching FBS when I became frightened after seeing a large crowd. While trying to brake, I mistakenly pressed the accelerator. The car began moving at high speed and hit several students in front of me. The driver later helped bring it under control,” he said.
Eyewitnesses also said angry students beat two people who were in the car and vandalized the vehicle after the accident.
Sadman’s father, Dr Mohammad Shahidul Islam, said he would accept whatever decision the university authorities made regarding the incident.
DU Proctor Associate Professor Dr Md Israfil Ratan said he had been informed of the accident and that arrangements had been made for the injured students’ treatment.
“Some students fell from rickshaws. Arrangements have been made for their treatment. We were fortunate that there was no major accident,” he said.

item.title: Humaiun Kobir to attend 7th CICA Summit in Baku on Thursday
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir will visit Azerbaijan and Iraq this week as part of the government's efforts to promote peace, security and stability in Asia and beyond.
He will participate in a high-level meeting of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The CICA is a multinational forum for enhancing cooperation towards promoting peace, security and stability in Asia.
“I am going to Azerbaijan. I will be there from October 15 to 16,” Kobir told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday.
The 7th Summit of the CICA will be held on Thursday, a senior official told UNB, adding that the state minister is scheduled to leave Dhaka at 2am on Wednesday.
CICA Chairmanship of Azerbaijan will host the Summit with the support of the CICA Secretariat.
Heads of state or government, delegates from CICA member states, observer states, observer and partner organizations will participate in the event.
The 7th CICA Summit will bring together regional leaders to reaffirm their shared commitment to dialogue, mutual trust and constructive cooperation.
The event provides a vital platform for strengthening confidence-building measures, promoting peace, security, stability and sustainable development, as well as advancing multilateral approaches to addressing issues of common interest.
Highlighting the strategic importance of the visit, Kobir said Bangladesh now needs to develop greater engagement with Central Asia, describing the region as a new space and dimension for the country’s foreign policy outreach.
“Central Asia is a new space and dimension from the foreign policy projection point of view, and we are building engagement there,” he said.
The state minister said Bangladesh sees considerable scope for expanding political, economic and strategic engagement with the Central Asian countries as Dhaka seeks to diversify its external relations.
Following his Azerbaijan engagement, Kobir said he will travel to Baghdad, Iraq, to attend a meeting of Foreign Ministers of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) on Saturday.
He will also deliver a statement on behalf of Bangladesh at the OIC meeting.
The state minister said Bangladesh attaches importance to the Baghdad gathering at a time when significant geopolitical changes are taking place across the Middle East.
Referring to Iraq’s transformation after decades of conflict and instability, he said a new horizon for development and international engagement is emerging in the country.
“Baghdad is an interesting place to be at this time. After going through turbulent times over the last 20 years, a new space of opportunity and engagement has opened up,” Kobir said.
He said Bangladesh will explore possibilities for further engagement with Iraq as well as the wider region as countries affected by prolonged instability gradually enter a new phase.
The state minister underscored Bangladesh’s strong interest in peace and stability in the Middle East, noting that the region is home to a huge number of Bangladeshi expatriate workers.
“Peace and stability in the Middle East are of interest to Bangladesh. We have nearly eight million workers there and a very large workforce,” he said.
Their safety, welfare and well-being remain among the government’s highest priorities, particularly amid conflicts and security threats in different parts of the region, Kobir added.
He said instability in the Middle East could have implications not only for Bangladeshi expatriates but also for the country’s economic and energy interests.
The state minister said numerous diplomatic and informal channels are currently engaged in efforts to find peaceful solutions to regional conflicts.
“Many stakeholders are formally and diplomatically engaged to bring about a peaceful resolution. There are also informal and back-channel discussions,” he said.
Kobir said Bangladesh, with its long-standing experience and internationally recognised role in UN peacekeeping, will positively consider any proposal to contribute to safeguarding peace and stability in the Middle East.
“We will always positively consider any proposal that comes to Bangladesh to participate in safeguarding peace and stability in the Middle East and beyond,” he said.

item.title: Zverev defies 'physical issues' to reach Shanghai quarters
item.description:
Top-seeded Alexander Zverev toughed out two tie-breaks to beat Alexander Bublik 7-6 (8/6), 4-6, 7-6 (7/1) at the Shanghai Masters on Tuesday, winning his first match since being guaranteed the year-end world number one ranking.
The 29-year-old German will play Alex de Minaur in the quarter-finals.
"Really difficult match," Zverev said.
"I had some physical issues so, you know, I was maybe slower," he told the crowd.
"My ankle was acting up unfortunately again," Zverev elaborated in an on-court interview, without giving specifics.
"I'm starting to feel my body more, but happy to be through."
Zverev, the current world number two, was guaranteed the year-end number one spot after third-ranked Carlos Alcaraz lost to Zizou Bergs in Shanghai on Monday.
On Tuesday, Zverev called the honour "special", saying it was a different feeling to winning tournaments, adding he was "looking forward" to the responsibility of owning that status.
Neither player could create much trouble for his opponent in the first set as they traded aces to hold serve.

item.title: Carvajal joins Getafe until end of season
item.description:
Former Real Madrid defender Dani Carvajal signed for Getafe on Tuesday as a free agent until the end of the season.
The 34-year-old right-back left Los Blancos, with whom he won 27 trophies, at the end of last season.
"Getafe have reached a deal with Dani Carvajal that will keep him at the club until 30 June 2027," said the LaLiga side in a statement, highlighting his "leadership and experience".
Carvajal came through Real Madrid's La Fabrica youth academy and, after he left for Bayer Leverkusen in 2012, returned to the Spanish giants the following summer.
The defender was hampered by injury for much of last season and was not called up to join Spain's squad as La Roja won the World Cup.

item.title: Formula One to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' in Rwanda
item.description:
Rwanda will host Africa's first Formula One Grand Prix since 1993 in "the early 2030s" after the circuit announced a decade-long deal with the country on Tuesday.
The East African nation has been chasing a Grand Prix race for years, having already used football, basketball and other sports to enhance its image and attract investment.
President Paul Kagame formally announced the bid when Rwanda hosted a gathering of the FIA in December 2024.
The last time an F1 race was held in Africa was the 33rd South African Grand Prix, won by Alain Prost 33 years ago.
The first African Grand Prix in Rwanda will take place "once a new purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, Rwanda, has been completed", F1 said in a statement.
"Today is a landmark moment for Formula One," F1 president Stefano Domenicali added.
"With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.
"Africa has always been part of Formula One's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
A landlocked country still widely associated with a horrific genocide in 1994, Rwanda has used sports to revamp its image, attract tourists and impress investors with its organisational efficiency.
It has spent lavishly on football sponsorship deals with clubs including Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain, partnered with the NBA to be the main hub of its African basketball league, and hosted last year's cycling world championships.
'Today belongs to Africa' Critics have called this "sports-washing" -- using glitzy events to distract from accusations of serious human rights abuses, including a brutal crackdown on any opposition or dissent.
Others see that as Western hypocrisy, arguing no one described this year's World Cup in the United States as "sports-washing", despite the country's rights abuses.
"Today belongs to Africa," said Kagame.
"For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement."
"This partnership is long overdue, but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent, especially for African fans.
"Ultimately, what we want is for the African Grand Prix to pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent. This is not impossible to achieve, and what we are doing proves this."
The announcement will delight one of F1's biggest stars, Lewis Hamilton.
The seven-time world champion has long called for an African stop on the F1 circuit, backing Rwanda's plans in 2024 and calling the country "one of my favourite places".
South Africa had also been bidding to host an F1 race, and its sports minister emphasised last week it should not be ruled out.
"(Rwanda) have worked on it longer than (South Africa) and deserve it," South Africa's sports minister Gayton McKenzie posted on X last Thursday after the expected Rwanda deal was reported.
"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two F1s a year, and some react like a continent of 55 countries can only get one." He predicted that "SA will get F1, even before 2030."

item.title: Netflix wins Spain TV rights for 2030 World Cup
item.description:
Streaming platform Netflix will broadcast all 104 matches of the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra, the company announced on Tuesday.
‘(We) will offer all 104 matches of the world’s biggest football competition live,’ Netflix said in a statement.
Spain, the reigning champions, will co-host the tournament with Portugal and Morocco, while Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay will host matches to mark the centenary of the World Cup.
Under the agreement, one match per match-day will be available to watch free of charge in Spain, Netflix said.
A national free-to-air television channel in Spain will also broadcast all of the Spain’s matches and the final, along with other games, the company confirmed.
The deal marks another step in Netflix’s expansion into live sports as it competes with traditional broadcasters.
It will be the first time the subscription-based platform broadcasts the men’s World Cup.
Netflix already holds the rights to broadcast the 2027 and 2031 editions of the women’s World Cup in the United States and Canada.

item.title: Hazlewood takes six as Australia win first Test Durban
item.description:
Josh Hazlewood took six wickets as Australia completed a 214-run win over South Africa on the fifth day of the first Test at Kingsmead on Tuesday.
Fast bowler Hazlewood twice broke promising stands and finished with six for 49.
The hosts, set 421 runs to win, were bowled out for 206, in the first Test series between the teams in South Africa since the 2018 sandpaper scandal.
Opening batsman Aiden Markram defied the bowlers for a minute short of six hours, scoring 75 before he was ninth out, caught behind from an inside edge off Mitchell Starc.
The last four wickets fell for five runs in the space of 16 deliveries against the second new ball.
Markram and Wiaan Mulder (29) were largely untroubled as they batted through the first 110 minutes of the day.
But a double bowling change brought two wickets.
Mulder was caught down the legside by wicketkeeper Alex Carey off Hazlewood for 29 after a 139-minute innings during which he faced 110 balls.
Man of the match Matt Renshaw came on to bowl his off-spinners in the next over and with his first ball dismissed Kyle Verreynne for a single when the South African wicketkeeper played a forcing shot against a wide ball and edged a catch to Steve Smith at slip.
It was the continuation of a dream match for Renshaw, who top-scored in both innings with 190 and 82, then took his first Test wicket when he dismissed South African captain Temba Bavuma on Monday.
It was Smith's fifth catch of a match in which he became the world record-holder for most catches by a fielder in Tests.
Smith was back in action after being off the field at the start of South Africa's innings on Monday following a blow on the head while batting.
Marco Jansen made 35 and added 45 with Markram before Hazlewood bowled him in the fourth over with the second new ball. Three balls later Simon Harmer gloved a sharply lifting ball to Carey.
Australia were in trouble at 124 for six on the first day but dominated the rest of the match after Renshaw steered them to a first innings total of 390.

item.title: Afghanistan bat out 142 overs to deny Bangladesh victory
item.description:
Afghanistan batted for 142 overs to save the one-off Test against Bangladesh in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday.
They finished on 346 for eight after spending the final day fighting to avoid defeat.
Sediqullah Atal led the resistance with his maiden Test century, scoring 111 off 332 balls, while Qais Ahmad struck two sixes in the final over to cap a tense finish.
Afghanistan had been set a target of 479 and needed to survive the day after resuming at 132 for three.
Bangladesh had put themselves in a strong position by taking a 106-run first-innings lead. They scored 346 before dismissing Afghanistan for 240, then declared their second innings at 372 for seven.
Atal, who had scored 35 not out at the end of the fourth day, continued to frustrate Bangladesh’s bowlers. His innings included nine fours and three sixes.
Rahmat Shah made 51 off 124 balls before Ebadot Hossain had him caught behind by Litton Das. Hashmatullah Shahidi added 36, while Ikram Alikhil scored 33.
Bangladesh kept taking wickets but could not finish the job. Ebadot claimed three for 50 and Mehidy Hasan Miraz took three for 73.
Taijul Islam finally removed Atal in the 119th over, leaving Afghanistan at 281 for seven and giving Bangladesh a chance to dismiss the tail.
But Afghanistan’s lower order held on. Bangladesh missed two run-out opportunities and Hasan Mahmud dropped a catch, allowing the visitors to extend their resistance.
Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for his 19 before falling to Miraz. Zia-ur-Rehman then helped see out the remaining overs, while Qais, struggling with hamstring cramps, remained unbeaten on 49 off 80 balls.
With the draw assured in the final over, Qais launched Taijul for two sixes, the second clearing deep midwicket off the last ball.
Afghanistan’s 142 overs of batting made this one of the longest fourth-innings rearguards in Test cricket by a team saving a draw.

item.title: The power of speaking up
item.description:
Psychological safety in the workplace refers to an environment where employees feel confident and secure enough to speak openly and spontaneously about issues the organization faces, particularly when making business decisions or responding to challenges arising from its internal and external business environment.
It encourages employees to express their views, concerns, ideas, and constructive criticism without fear of intimidation, retaliation, or negative consequences.
The scope of psychological safety should not be limited to interactions among peers and subordinates; it should also extend upward, creating an environment where employees feel confident to share constructive ideas, valuable information, and honest feedback with senior management.
Such ideas and information should, of course, be directed toward enhancing organizational well-being, effectiveness, and productivity.
However, one of the key challenges is that senior management may often be reluctant to encourage or accept such upward communication, which can discourage employees from speaking up and undermine the very essence of psychological safety.
Mistakes made by subordinate employees should be treated by superiors as opportunities for learning and improvement, while maintaining respect and dignity for those involved.
To foster such an environment, employees should not feel compelled to hide or avoid reporting mistakes, as concealing errors may have more serious consequences and adversely affect important business decisions.
In this context, emotional intelligence can serve as an important bridge between employees and management, enabling both sides to respond to mistakes with empathy, maturity, and constructive communication, thereby strengthening trust and psychological safety throughout the organization.
Management has a responsibility to foster a supportive and respectful work environment where employees feel psychologically safe to share their knowledge, expertise, ideas, and concerns.
This requires moving away from a culture of intimidation, fear, and silence that may have persisted for years, and instead creating an atmosphere of trust where employees are encouraged to speak openly and contribute their knowledge for the betterment of the organization.
Employee engagement can be significantly enhanced by fostering psychological safety in the workplace, which can also serve as a gateway to developing future leaders within the organization.
HR professionals have an important role to play in encouraging employees to speak up, share ideas, express concerns, and contribute constructively. When employees feel heard and valued, they are more likely to become engaged, take initiative, and demonstrate leadership potential -- ultimately contributing to higher productivity and the long-term success of the organization.
There are several approaches and mechanisms that can foster psychological safety and enable employees to participate confidently in the decision-making process. These may include open-forum discussions, seminars, formal and informal meetings, interactive sessions, employee feedback platforms, and other participatory initiatives.
The human resources division can play a pivotal role in designing and facilitating such initiatives, thereby creating an environment where employees feel encouraged to express their views, share ideas, and contribute meaningfully to organizational decisions.
However, creating an environment of psychological safety is not without challenges. Reluctance or lack of openness among senior management, fear of unwanted punishment or negative consequences, excessive pressure from supervisors, and concerns about potential external threats may discourage employees from speaking openly and expressing their views.
Unless these barriers are addressed through supportive leadership, mutual trust, and a non-intimidating workplace culture, the organization may find it difficult to establish genuine psychological safety.
Bimal Chandra Roy is Company Secretary, North-West Power Generation Company Ltd. Email: cs@nwpgcl.gov.bd .

item.title: Who are we writing for?
item.description:
Every columnist eventually confronts a question more unsettling than the blank page: Who, exactly, are we writing for?
We write about corruption, inequality, and political hypocrisy. We defend the vulnerable, question the powerful, and imagine better possibilities.
Then we publish, share the link, receive a handful of reactions, and return to our lives.
The next morning, the powerful remain powerful, and yesterday's injustices compete with newer ones for attention.
Has the column made a difference or merely supplied content to an insatiable machine?
This is not simply a crisis of readership. It is a crisis of purpose.
The question is not only whether people read our words, but whether words can interrupt the habits of a society that has learned to live comfortably with its contradictions.
Attention has become a commodity. A political scandal is consumed alongside celebrity gossip, a humanitarian catastrophe beside a dance video, and an argument between advertisements.
The thumb moves before the mind finishes thinking. A tragedy appears, provokes outrage, and disappears beneath a joke. Even suffering has become content, with a short life expectancy.
The newspaper column faces an existential disadvantage. It asks for patience: Staying with an uncomfortable argument, entertaining competing explanations and resisting immediate verdicts.
Yet the dominant culture rewards speed, certainty, and spectacle. Nuance is difficult to package. Doubt is equally difficult to monetize. A qualified argument rarely travels as far as a sharpened accusation.
Neil Postman warned in Amusing Ourselves to Death that public discourse could become entertainment, sacrificing substance to spectacle.
The danger is not that people have stopped receiving information, but that it arrives in forms discouraging reflection. We know more, with less time to understand.
Does this mean the columnist is fighting a losing battle? Perhaps, but that conclusion is premature.
We err when we measure writing only through readership figures, shares, comments, and institutional responses. These reveal circulation, not consequence.
A column may reach thousands and change nobody's mind. Another may stay with one reader long enough to alter a decision, challenge prejudice, or encourage resistance to injustice.
We rarely know which sentence will live again in a classroom, newsroom, or family dispute. An argument's public life may be invisible to its author.
John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty , defended contesting opinions because even an unpopular or mistaken view can force prevailing beliefs to justify themselves rather than survive through habit.
Our responsibility is not necessarily immediate consensus or reform. It is to resist stagnation when questions become too inconvenient to ask.
A society becomes unjust when people lose the language to recognize injustice. Wrongdoing disguises itself: Exploitation becomes efficiency, exclusion necessity, censorship responsibility, and opportunism pragmatism.
The columnist exposes these transformations and restores the names power tries to change.
George Orwell understood the political significance of language. In Politics and the English Language , he argued that corrupted language can facilitate political manipulation and intellectual dishonesty.
Writing, therefore, is not merely expressing an opinion. At its best, it makes reality harder to disguise. A good column does not simply tell readers what to think; it helps them recognize what they have been encouraged not to see.
Writers must confront an uncomfortable possibility: Sometimes we write less to change the world than to reassure ourselves that we have taken a position.
Outrage becomes a professional identity, renewed weekly without demanding much of its owner. We condemn public hypocrisy while cultivating vanity, criticizing political performance while performing righteousness for an audience.
Writing about injustice does not make a writer virtuous. A column may defend the poor for vanity, turn people into symbols or reduce reality to a politically useful narrative. Moral authority rests not on declared intentions but on honesty, discipline, and willingness to confront inconvenient evidence.
Albert Camus, in The Rebel , explored the moral tension between resistance and its limits. Rebellion becomes dangerous when defending human dignity turns into justification for new domination.
Opposition alone does not guarantee moral clarity. We must question not only the injustices committed by those we oppose but also those we excuse when they serve our preferred cause.
This matters in societies where political loyalties determine the boundaries of outrage. A columnist who condemns an offense when committed by one political camp but rationalizes the same offense when committed by another is not defending a principle. The columnist is defending a tribe.
Consistency is less glamorous than indignation, but it is the foundation of credibility.
So, whom are we writing for? Not necessarily for millions who may never encounter our work, nor exclusively for officials who might respond to criticism.
We write for readers willing to think beyond inherited assumptions, for those whose doubts have not found language, and for those who need to know that discomfort with public injustice is neither irrational nor solitary.
We also write for a future reader who may return to the record and ask who noticed, who objected, who remained silent, and what arguments were available when society made its choices.
Hannah Arendt's reflections on responsibility and judgment matter here. In Eichmann in Jerusalem and her broader political writings, she examined the dangers of thoughtlessness and the failure to exercise independent moral judgment.
Public writing can resist that failure. A columnist cannot think on behalf of readers, but can create conditions in which thought becomes harder to evade.
Nor should we romanticize the profession. A column is not organizing a community, building an institution, or changing a law. An elegant article cannot substitute for justice, and a thousand condemnations cannot replace accountability. Writers must not confuse describing a problem with solving it.
Writing is one part of civic life. A column can preserve evidence, challenge official narratives, clarify neglected questions, and keep an issue alive after its commercial appeal fades.
In Four Quartets , TS Eliot writes: "For us, there is only the trying. The rest is not our business." This is no excuse for carelessness. Writers must test their accuracy, reach beyond the already convinced and reflect the realities they describe.
Yet honest speech's consequences cannot always be controlled by its speaker.
Perhaps the question is whether we would continue writing if applause disappeared, readership declined, and critics never acknowledged us. The point is not to ignore readers, but to distinguish communication from the desire to be admired.
The danger of doomscrolling is not simply that readers forget yesterday's arguments. Writers may adapt to the same forgetfulness, producing louder opinions for shorter attention spans.
When every column must become spectacle to survive, the writer risks becoming another entertainer in the marketplace of outrage.
We cannot compel society to listen, but we can refuse to measure our work by distraction.
We can write precisely instead of exaggerating, remain fair instead of partisan, and return to neglected questions after novelty moves on.
Perhaps, sometimes, we are creating empty noise. No profession is immune to vanity, repetition, or futility. But silence is not automatically wisdom, and the absence of immediate change does not prove an argument has failed.
Between the illusion that writing can save the world and the cynicism that writing can do nothing lies a harder responsibility: Speak truthfully, question relentlessly, and remain answerable to the people whose lives our words describe.
The columnist may never know who was listening. The more important question is whether, amid the noise, the columnist was still saying something worth hearing.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: ‘We’re not giving up:’ Activist Thunberg joins France student protests
item.description:
Thousands of protesters marched through central Paris on Tuesday as part of nationwide demonstrations supporting high school pupils who have been protesting for better classroom conditions, with Swedish activist Greta Thunberg taking part.
With just six months to go before elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron, French authorities had been hoping that the protests were easing ahead of half-term holidays starting at the end of this week.
But teenagers at high schools called lycees -- backed by university students, teachers, unions and the far-left opposition party France Unbowed (LFI) -- have said their demands have not been met.
French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among the crowd of demonstrators in Paris.
Outside the Paris city hall, demonstrators -- mostly university students -- gathered in the early afternoon to the tune of an orchestra playing the Rebel Fanfare from the Star Wars movies.
“I’m expecting a surge of solidarity,” said 20-year-old Patricia, not wishing to give her surname.
“We’re not giving up the fight, whether it’s for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence,” she added, referencing multiple allegations of police brutality against protesters in recent weeks.
The education ministry said 214 schools were closed on Tuesday. Most of these were high schools out of the country’s 3,700.
University student union l’Union Etudiante reported that 90 percent of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
Thunberg, who became famous as a teen for school strikes to demand action on climate change, stood among pupils demonstrating outside a school in the capital’s largest suburb, Saint-Denis.
“Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” the 23-year-old told reporters outside the Paul Eluard high school.
French students say they are determined to press their demands for solutions to too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances.
The protests, launched late last month, have seen teenagers pile up dumpsters and security barriers outside hundreds of lycees.
Rallies were also underway in other cities on Tuesday.
In the western city of Nantes, thousands marched behind a banner reading “Schools without money, a country without a future.”
“I think there are a lot of us in France who are still motivated,” 16-year-old Mariolino said.
“Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don’t get it.”
In the northeastern city of Strasbourg, Adeline Ferier, 42, a middle school French teacher, said she was demonstrating to support her 16-year-old daughter.
“I think it’s great that young people are aware of inequalities and are getting involved,” she said.
More than 70,000 people took to the streets last Thursday in the last major event of the movement.
The demonstrations in recent weeks have mostly been peaceful, but clashes have occasionally broken out with police.
More than 6,800 people -- largely minors -- have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the justice ministry.
Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff members have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
Authorities said fireworks fired through tubes on Monday injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille.
Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.
Macron, speaking to reporters at a car show on Monday, urged restraint from protesters.
“These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said just months before elections to replace him.
After last week’s nationwide demonstrations, the government promised that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
The education minister said on Tuesday that 35 percent had already been assigned.
High school students are demanding a $11 billion boost for lycees.

item.title: Indonesia wildfire burns homes, displaces hundreds
item.description:
A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday, as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in the Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, mayor Riza Herdavid told reporters.
“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
“My house is gone,” Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything,” said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
Another survivor, Haryanti, said strong winds had fueled the flames, which ravaged homes made mostly of wood.
“I immediately ran to save myself. None of my belongings survived... only the clothes on my back,” the 50-year-old homemaker told AFP.
Mayor Riza said the village was built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, converted into a housing complex last year.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year because of the drought-causing El Nino weather phenomenon, set to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo islands.
This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia.
To make matters worse, thick smoke in a province of Borneo has grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts to battle wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.
Cabinet secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to combat fires on the ground.

item.title: Red Cross calls for urgent de-escalation in Middle East
item.description:
The Red Cross called Tuesday for urgent de-escalation in the Middle East, warning that further fighting would be disastrous for tens of millions of civilians.
Yemen’s civil war -- in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis -- reignited in July, months into the wider regional conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
“Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” said Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The Houthis quickly began targeting Saudi oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs, including a string of lethal strikes on Riyadh’s airport, rocking the world’s top oil exporter.
“The deaths, injuries and destruction in Saudi Arabia in recent days are yet another example of the devastating toll that hostilities are taking on civilians,” Spoljaric said in a statement.
“In Yemen, the scale of death, displacement and damage to civilian infrastructure, including in Aden and Sana’a, is mounting at an alarming rate. Across the Middle East, civilian infrastructure has repeatedly been hit and lives have been lost,” the ICRC chief added.
Spoljaric said civilians and civilian objects had to be spared from attack, while parties to conflict must, at all times, distinguish between civilians, civilian objects and military targets.
Strikes on ports, airports and essential infrastructure risk severe consequences for communities who rely on them, she added.
“A further intensification of hostilities would be disastrous for tens of millions of people. Urgent efforts must be made to de-escalate and protect civilians from further harm,” Spoljaric said.
The long-running Yemeni civil war has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.
The Geneva-based ICRC acts as the guardians of international humanitarian law, the set of rules which seeks to limit the effects of armed conflict.
It protects people who are not or are no longer participating in hostilities and restricts the means and methods of warfare.

item.title: Jamaat leader Taher condemns harassment of Prof Yunus at US airport
item.description:
Deputy Opposition Leader and Jamaat-e-Islami Nayeb-e-Ameer Syed Abdullah Mohammed Taher on Tuesday strongly condemned the harassment of Nobel laureate and former interim government chief adviser Prof Muhammad Yunus at New York’s John F Kennedy (JFK) International Airport.
In a statement, he said some associates of "Awami fascists" harassed Prof Yunus using indecent language at the airport.
He termed the incident unacceptable and highly condemnable.
He said the harassment of the Nobel laureate, who is respected internationally humiliated not only Bangladesh’s citizens but also the country as a whole on the global stage.
He said such shameful acts against respected Bangladeshis on foreign soil are inappropriate and undermine the country’s dignity and honour internationally.
He urged everyone to refrain from such behaviour to uphold Bangladesh’s reputation abroad.
He further alleged that the ousted Awami League’s “fascist forces” continued conspiring against Bangladesh and its people from abroad after being driven out of the country.
He also accused them of undermining the security of expatriate Bangladeshis and patriotic citizens travelling overseas.
He expressed confidence that peace-loving people in Bangladesh and expatriates would resist such conspiracies and continue working for the country’s welfare.
He also called on officials at Bangladesh’s embassies and high commissions abroad to take responsible and courageous steps in this regard.

item.title: Colleges asked to finalise Class XI enrolment by October 15
item.description:
Colleges must complete the admission process for students who confirmed their places online for Class XI in the 2026–27 academic year by 5:00pm on October 15, according to a directive from the Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee.
The directive was issued in a notice signed on Monday by committee president and Dhaka Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Chairman Professor Syed Anwaruzzaman.
Under the directive, colleges must log in to the Class XI admission website using their Educational Institution Identification Number (EIIN) and password, verify the required documents of selected students and finalise their admissions through the online system.
The documents include proof of eligibility under the FQ, EQ-1, EQ-2 and SQ quotas. Colleges must verify the documents before confirming the admissions of eligible students.
The notice warned that the board would not be responsible for any complications arising from failure to complete admissions within the deadline.
